6. Mr Md Kamruzzaman Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the learned Joint District Judge erred in law in not appreciating the provisions of section 17A and 17B of the Registration Act. It has been clearly depicted from those section that if an unregistered contract for sale executed prior to section 17A if it is not presented for registration within 6 months from the date of coming into force the provision of law of section 17A and 17B of the Registration Act, after expiry of six months the said contract for sale shall stand void. Moreover, subject to the provision of section 17A of the Registration Act a contract for sale of immovable property shall be in writing and registered one. But in the instant case by the plaintiffs neither claimed for unregistered contract nor they have any written contract, rather they claimed the property as oral contract and filed the suit which is practically impossible to get registration of the deed in question. He has further added that the suit is barred by the provisions of law of limitation Act as per the provision of the amended Article 113 of the Limitation Act, a suit for specific performance of contract has to be filed within 1 (one) year from the date fixed. However, the suit has been filed in the year 2008. The contract was made in 1996. So, it is crystal clear that the suit is barred by law of limitation. He has further pointed out that he has taken a ground to the effect that according to the provisions of section 21A of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 the Court below has passed the impugned order in violation of the provision of the said section and, as such, the same is liable to be set-aside and plaint is liable to be rejected. He has further pointed out that the provisions of section 21A of the Specific Relief Act have clarified the position who will get specific performance of contract.  8. On the other hand, Mr Md Mokarramus Shaklan for Mr JN Deb, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 pointed that the learned Advocate for the petitioners although pointed the period of limitation regarding filing of the suit. However, he replied that the period of limitation would be counted from the date of refusal as there is no specific stipulation regarding the period of limitation. Mr Md Kamruzzaman Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate for the petitioners has referred Article 113 of the Limitation Act and submitted that the earlier limitation was for specific performance of contract for 3(three) years and now after amendment it becomes 1 (one) year and, as such, the suit is hopelessly barred by law of limitation. Again Mr Shaklan replied the question that since there is no specific stipulation or written contract the limitation under the said Article it would not be applicable for the instant case. Mr Shaklan has further pointed out that the case is an exceptional one because the fact remains that the father of the plaintiff and defendants himself negotiated the transaction in between his children wherein 2 were minors. Therefore, he took the money for consideration of the property in his own name and made a bond where two minors were nominated as his legal representatives in the Islami Bank, Sylhet Branch as consideration of the sale of property. So, it would be crystal clear that the possession of the suit property was handed over to the plaintiffs in presence of their father and other witnesses. However, in respect of transaction there was no written or registered instrument as his father was the negotiator of the transaction it was an absolute real contract. So, as regards sections 17A and 17B of the Registration Act, 1908 do not come into effect in the instant case, because the provision of law has clearly depicted the restriction in respect of registry of the unregistered instrument not for oral contract. Mr Shaklan further pointed that the learned Advocate for the petitioners although pointed from the plaint and from the power of attorney that the power of attorney was not given for registration of the property in favour of the plaintiffs. However, he pointed that there is a language in the power of attorney, amongst other properties the suit property may be transferred which was empowered by the principal to the agent. Therefore, the plaintiffs requested the defendant No. 4 the attorney of the principal defendants who lived in UK to register the documents in favour of them. However, he refused on a certain date and, as such, from that date of refusal the cause of action has been arisen to file the instant suit. 

 10. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned order, the application for rejection of the plaint and the plaint of the suit. It appears from the impugned order that the Court below opined that there is some exceptional materials in the plaint which deserves for examination through evidence. The trial Court also opined that since it is a contract in between the son and father as guardian of minor kids as oral contract but the law has given restriction for the parties to register the unregistered contract within specific period. But in respect of oral contract which does not come within the ambit of sections 17A and 17B of the Registration Act, 1908 and, as such, rejected the application for rejection of the plaint. From the arguments launched by the learned Advocates of both the parties, it appears to us that the learned Advocates of the petitioner have tried to point out some legal errors in the impugned order. However, on perusal of the impugned order we are of view that the Court below did not commit any legal error in passing the impugned order. It is also depicted from the facts and circumstances of the case that the transaction was made in between the step-brothers through their father and the matter was negotiated by their father. Out of three defendants two were minors and for that purpose there was a bond in the name of the father, who nominated the two minors as legal nominees as the consideration money of the suit property. However, we are of the view that whether the suit is maintainable or not that would be decided after examining the evidence. But on a plain reading of the plaint we do not find any ground or it is not suggestive that the suit is barred by any law of limitation including sections 17A and 17B of the Registration Act, 1908 as pointed by the learned Advocate for the petitioners. Moreover it appears to us that the principal defendants are not unwilling to give the registered deed rather they have appointed Attorney for that purpose as they are living in UK who is unwilling and refused to give registered deed and contested in the case. Therefore we are of the view that it is a good case which to be decided after taking evidence.
